h: Coast paths, a maypole and Belfast close by
p: Two or three hours is a good amount of time for the Transport Museum, though train fans could easily stretch it further. If you're also planning the Folk Museum on the same estate, think about splitting them across a full day, or even two separate visits, so nobody runs out of steam halfway round.

Holywood itself has a couple of claims to fame. A maypole stands in the middle of the town, said to be the only permanent one in Ireland, and it's become a much-loved landmark. Golf fans will know the town as the home of Rory McIlroy, who learned his game at Holywood Golf Club.

Want some fresh air after all those engines? The North Down Coastal Path runs from Holywood along the shore of Belfast Lough towards Bangor. Cultra sits right on the route, so you can walk a section and enjoy views of the shipping on the lough. Further along, Crawfordsburn Country Park has a beach, woodland paths and a waterfall, perfect for a family ramble.

Belfast is only a short drive or train ride away, and that opens up a whole extra day. Titanic Belfast, in the city's Titanic Quarter, tells the story of the famous liner built in the shipyards here, and it pairs brilliantly with the transport theme. Bangor, the other way along the coast, has a marina, a seafront and a range of places to eat.
